t: Lantern Festival: six roads to close as 320,000 visitors expected next weekend
s: Riverside Avenue will shut to traffic for nine hours on both days of the 68th Springvale Lantern Festival, there will be no festival parking, and Vale Rail will run ten extra trains each evening. Organisers will decide on Thursday whether the typhoon changes any plans.
x: Drivers in central Springvale face the city's largest road closures of the year next weekend, when the 68th Springvale Lantern Festival returns to the banks of the Mirror River on Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October. The Springvale Lantern Festival Executive Committee and Springvale Central Police Station on Friday published the traffic plan for the two days. Six roads will close or be restricted, the longest closure being Riverside Avenue, which shuts to all vehicles, bicycles included, between Nishiki Bridge and Asahi Bridge from 14:00 to 23:00 on both days. The committee expects about 320,000 visitors, up from 304,000 last year, as the number of lanterns rises to 12,000 from 11,000. The programme is the same on both days. Stalls open along the 1.3 km riverside promenade at 16:00 and the lanterns in Castle Park, on Komachi-dori and along the river are lit from 17:30. At 18:00 a lantern procession leaves Springvale Castle and makes its way down to the river at Nishiki Bridge by 20:30. From 19:30 to 21:00, lanterns are floated on the river from the riverside steps below Nishiki Bridge, beside the main stage near Castle Town Station. The festival closes at 21:00. Which roads close, and when Komachi-dori, the old-town street that runs 650 metres from the Castle Park east gate to the North Exit of Springvale Central Station, becomes pedestrian-only from 12:00 to 22:00 on both days. Shops on the street can take deliveries until 11:30. Nishiki Bridge closes to vehicles from 16:00 to 22:00 each day. From 19:00 to 21:00 on both evenings, walkers on the bridge will only be able to cross from north to south, to keep people moving during the lantern floating below. Asahi Bridge stays open but is reduced to a single northbound lane from 15:00 to 23:00. Otemachi-dori, between the Castle Park south gate and Nishiki Bridge, closes from 17:30 to 21:00 on both days for the lantern procession, which runs from 18:00 to 20:30. The road in front of Castle Town Station, from the station square at the River Exit down to Riverside Avenue, is closed to vehicles from 17:00 to 22:00. We are asking everyone, residents included, to leave the car at home. The riverside cannot take traffic and 300,000 people at the same time. — Haruo Tanabe, chair of the executive committee No parking: use the park-and-ride There will be no festival car parks in the centre, and the police say cars stopping on Riverside Avenue before 14:00 will be towed. Instead, two park-and-ride sites open from 15:00: the Springvale University Kita Campus car park, with 1,200 spaces, and Ferry Port Car Park No. 2, with 800. Both charge ¥500 per car, which covers the shuttle bus for everyone in it. Shuttles run every 10 minutes from 15:00 to 22:30 to the Castle Park east gate. Cyclists can use a temporary bicycle park for 1,500 bikes in the grounds of Shiroyama Elementary School, a ten-minute walk from the riverside. Springvale City runs a wheelchair viewing area near the North Exit of Springvale Central Station; places must be booked with the city in advance. City buses on routes 3, 5 and 12 will be diverted away from the river from 14:00 to 23:00 on both days. The city transport bureau says delays of up to 30 minutes are likely on other routes that cross the centre in the evening. Ten extra trains each evening Springvale Railway (Vale Rail) will run ten extra trains on both days, on top of its Saturday and holiday timetable. All of them stop at every station, and none appears in the station timetables or in Vale Rail's journey planner. On the Mirror Line, two extra trains bring visitors in from Clayfield, leaving at 17:20 and 18:20 and reaching Springvale Central at 17:43 and 18:43. Three late trains take them home: the 21:40 from Springvale Central to Clayfield (arriving 22:03), the 22:30 to Red Canyon (23:09) and the 23:25 to Clayfield (23:48). Each leaves Castle Town three minutes after Springvale Central. On the Bayside Line, five extra trains leave Springvale Central for Ferry Port at 21:15, 21:45, 22:15, 22:45 and 23:30; the last arrives at 23:58. The regular last trains from Springvale Central on both nights are the 22:15 to Moonview Spa and the 22:50 to Clayfield on the Mirror Line, and the 23:00 to Ferry Port and the 23:35 to Rose Garden on the Bayside Line. Castle Town, four minutes from the main stage by the River Exit, is expected to be the busiest station. Vale Rail says it may restrict entry there from 18:00 to 21:30, asking passengers to wait outside, and the station's coin lockers will be closed from 15:00. Limited express Comet 21, 24, 25 and 28 will not stop at Castle Town on either day. Springvale Central is a 20-minute walk along the river, and its North Exit is five minutes from the Asahi Bridge end of the promenade. The Comet peak surcharge of ¥200 applies from 10 to 12 October, and the Moonview Spa Day Ticket cannot be used on those days. Vale Rail advises visitors to charge their RideCard cards or buy return tickets before the evening: ticket machines at Springvale Central had queues of up to 40 minutes after the festival closed last year. (Vale Rail's new timetable starts on 14 November and does not affect the festival.) Festival at a glance Dates: Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October, the same programme on both days; stalls from 16:00, lanterns lit from 17:30, closing at 21:00 Lantern procession: 18:00–20:30, from Springvale Castle along Otemachi-dori to Nishiki Bridge Lantern floating: 19:30–21:00, Nishiki Bridge riverside steps by the main stage (3,000 floating lanterns, 1,500 each evening, ¥1,000, on sale until 9 October) Nearest stations: Castle Town (River Exit, 4 minutes; entry may be restricted 18:00–21:30) and Springvale Central (North Exit, 5 minutes) Park-and-ride: ¥500 per car; shuttles every 10 minutes, 15:00–22:30 Crowd sensors and 620 stewards After Nishiki Bridge became gridlocked for about 25 minutes during the floating lantern release last year, when 14 people were treated for minor injuries, the committee has doubled the number of stewards on the bridge. In all, 620 stewards and 180 police officers will be on duty, and 46 sensors on lamp posts will measure crowd density in real time as part of a trial with Springvale University. Drones are banned over the festival area. There are 140 registered food and craft stalls along the promenade, open from 16:00. Unregistered stalls will be asked to leave. What about the typhoon? Typhoon No. 21 is expected to pass close to Springvale early on Monday 5 October. The committee said the 4,000 lanterns already hung along the riverside would be taken down on Sunday morning and put back between 6 and 9 October. The festival is five days after the typhoon. Unless the riverside is damaged, we expect to go ahead as planned. — Haruo Tanabe The committee will announce on Thursday 8 October at 15:00 whether every event, including the lantern floating, goes ahead. Updates will appear on the festival website and in our live coverage of the typhoon.

t: 12,000 lanterns in 40 days: inside the Lantern Festival workshop
s: In a former textile warehouse in Riverside, 160 volunteers aged 9 to 87 are finishing the lanterns for the 68th Springvale Lantern Festival, 1,000 more than last year. Each one costs ¥1,850 and takes three days from bamboo to light.
x: The smell inside the former Riverside textile warehouse is of wheat-starch glue and damp paper. On long tables under the sawtooth roof, rows of bamboo frames wait for their skins, and along the back wall finished lanterns are stacked to the beams, white and blank, waiting for the evening of Saturday 10 October. Since 21 August, 160 volunteers have been making the 12,000 lanterns that will line the Mirror River, Castle Park and Komachi-dori during the 68th Springvale Lantern Festival on 10 and 11 October. That is 1,000 more than last year, and with ten days to go the workshop is turning out about 300 a day. "We are on schedule, just," said Fumiko Shimizu, 64, who has run the workshop for twelve years. "Every year the committee asks for more lanterns, every year I say we cannot do it, and then we do it." From bamboo to light in three days Each lantern begins as four strips of bamboo cut in winter from groves in the foothills of Mount Moonview and dried for six months. Volunteers bend and tie the strips into a frame about 45 cm tall, then paste on sheets of Moonview washi, a thick hand-made paper from a family workshop in the hills above Moonview Spa that has supplied the festival since the 1970s. The pasted lanterns dry for a day before an LED candle and a battery pack are fitted to the base. Real candles were dropped in 2019, after two lanterns on Nishiki Bridge caught fire in strong wind the year before. The LEDs flicker slowly, a setting the volunteers spent a whole winter choosing. "People said it would look cheap," Ms Shimizu said. "Nobody has noticed." Materials and batteries put the cost of each lantern at ¥1,850, or about ¥22 million for all 12,000. About a third of the frames are reused from last year; the rest are new. Aged 9 to 87 The oldest volunteer, Shigeru Hatano, is 87 and has worked on every festival since 1971, first as a carpenter building the river stages and, for the past 20 years, as the workshop's fastest frame-tier. He ties about 60 frames a day. The youngest is nine, a pupil at Riverside Elementary School who comes with her grandmother on Saturdays and is in charge of testing the LED candles. Most volunteers are retired, but the workshop has added evening sessions from 18:00 to 21:00 on weekdays for people with jobs, and 41 of this year's 160 come only in the evenings. I look for my grandson's lantern every year. Last year it was a train. This year he says it is a secret. — Shigeru Hatano, 87, volunteer Painted by 2,400 children Not every lantern is blank. In September, 2,400 lanterns went out to pupils at 38 elementary schools, who painted them on the theme "My river". The lanterns that came back, decorated with herons, yuzu, trains and at least one very large fish, will hang along the riverside between Nishiki Bridge and Asahi Bridge, each school on its own stretch marked by a numbered post so families can find them. 3,000 lanterns for the river A separate team makes the floating lanterns for the lantern floating, which runs from 19:30 to 21:00 on both evenings from the Nishiki Bridge riverside steps, beside the main stage near Castle Town Station. The 3,000 floating lanterns, 1,500 for each evening, have paper sides and a wooden base that break down in water, and nets at Minato Bridge collect them before they reach Harvest Bay. They are sold at ¥1,000 each, with a paper slip on which buyers write a wish or the name of someone they have lost, at four places in the city and online until 9 October or until they sell out. By Tuesday more than two-thirds had been sold, the executive committee said. Haruo Tanabe, 71, who chairs the committee, said the workshop was the part of the festival he worried about least. "The weather, the crowds, the trains: those keep me awake," he said. "The lanterns are always ready." Lantern facts 12,000 lanterns (11,000 in 2025), lit from 17:30 until the festival closes at 21:00 on 10 and 11 October 2,400 painted by pupils of 38 elementary schools Cost: ¥1,850 each; LED candles since 2019 3,000 floating lanterns (1,500 each evening) at ¥1,000, on sale until 9 October; floated 19:30–21:00 160 volunteers; work began on 21 August The Springvale City Museum of Art, which is showing four centuries of Springvale ware, will stay open until 21:00 on both festival evenings.

t: Lantern Festival to trial laser sensors that count people, not faces
s: Forty-six sensors on lamp posts along Riverside Avenue, Nishiki Bridge and Komachi-dori will alert stewards when crowds reach two people per square metre during next weekend's festival. Visitors will be able to check a live congestion map.
x: When the floating lanterns were released from below Nishiki Bridge at last year's Springvale Lantern Festival, the bridge above filled faster than stewards could clear it. For about 25 minutes nobody could move in either direction, and 14 people were treated for minor injuries. This year the bridge will be watched by machines as well as people. Springvale University and the city will trial 46 laser sensors, fixed to lamp posts on Riverside Avenue, Nishiki Bridge and Komachi-dori, that measure how densely people are packed and alert stewards before a crowd becomes dangerous. The trial covers both festival days, Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October. How the sensors work The sensors use lidar: they send out pulses of infrared laser light and time the reflections to build a three-dimensional cloud of points, refreshed ten times a second. Software developed in the laboratory of Professor Kenta Yoshimura, an information engineer at Springvale University, picks out the clusters of points that are people and counts them in each square metre of pavement. Unlike cameras, the sensors record no images, and the points cannot show a face, clothing or skin colour, Professor Yoshimura said. The counts are kept for 30 days for analysis and then deleted. A lidar sensor sees a person as about two hundred dots. It can tell you there are three people in a square metre. It cannot tell you who they are. — Professor Kenta Yoshimura, Springvale University Twelve sensors will be on Nishiki Bridge and its approaches, 24 along the 1.3 km of Riverside Avenue between Nishiki Bridge and Asahi Bridge, and 10 on Komachi-dori. Installation begins on Tuesday 6 October, once Typhoon No. 21 has passed, and the system will be tested on the evening of Thursday 8 October. Two thresholds The system works with two thresholds. When any section reaches two people per square metre, the stewards responsible for it receive an alert on their radios and phones and start directing people to other routes. At four people per square metre, entry to that section is stopped until the density falls. Crowd-safety researchers generally regard more than five people per square metre as dangerous, because people can no longer move freely and pressure builds through the crowd. The busiest hours are expected between 19:30 and 21:00 on both evenings, when lanterns are floated from the Nishiki Bridge riverside steps beside the main stage and the lantern procession from Springvale Castle reaches the river. Springvale Railway may restrict entry to Castle Town Station, four minutes from the main stage, from 18:00 to 21:30, and the control room will pass the readings for the bridge to station staff. The festival's 620 stewards and 180 police officers will be coordinated from a control room at City Hall, where the readings appear on a map of the festival area. Last year we had stewards shouting into radios that the bridge was full. By then it was already too late. We need to know five minutes earlier. — Hideki Saito, head of security, Lantern Festival Executive Committee A live map for visitors Visitors will see a simplified version. From 17:00 on both days, the festival website will show a live congestion map of the riverside, the bridge and Komachi-dori in three colours: green for under one person per square metre, yellow for one to two, and red above two. The map is updated every 30 seconds. Cost and privacy The trial costs ¥38 million and is paid for from the ¥0.3 billion set aside for festival safety in the city's September supplementary budget, which the council approved on 30 September. The same item pays for extra stewards and first-aid posts. The city's personal information review board approved the trial on 25 September, on condition that no camera is added to the sensors and that signs explain the system at every entrance to the festival area. Not everyone is convinced. "Today it is dots, tomorrow it could be cameras," said a member of a Shimo-Kawabata residents' group who attended a briefing for residents on Wednesday. Professor Yoshimura's team will publish its results by March 2027. If the trial works, the city says, the sensors could also be used at Springvale Central Station during large events and along the course of the Springvale Castle Marathon in February. The trial in numbers 46 lidar sensors: 12 on Nishiki Bridge, 24 on Riverside Avenue, 10 on Komachi-dori Stewards alerted at 2 people per m²; entry stopped at 4 people per m² Live map on the festival website from 17:00, updated every 30 seconds No images recorded; counts deleted after 30 days Cost: ¥38 million, from the September supplementary budget For road closures, park-and-ride and extra trains during the festival, see our festival travel guide.

t: Embankment works move downstream: 1.2 km of riverside path to close from 1 October
s: The second phase of Harvest Prefecture's ¥8.6 billion project to raise the Mirror River's left bank starts next Thursday. Walkers and cyclists will be diverted onto Minato-dori until about March 2028, and up to 140 lorries a day will use the road.
x: Five years after the Mirror River came over its banks at Shimo-Kawabata, the work to make sure it does not happen again is moving towards the sea. Harvest Prefecture said on Thursday that the second phase of its embankment works on the river's left bank will begin on 1 October, covering the 1.2 km between Minato Bridge and the river mouth. The riverside walking and cycling path along that stretch closes the same day and is not expected to reopen until about March 2028. The project, which began in April 2024, raises the crest of the embankment by 1.0 metre to 7.4 metres, drives steel sheet piles into the bank to stop water seeping through it, and adds a 12-metre-wide berm, a terrace on the land side that makes the bank harder to wash away. In all, 3.2 km of bank will be rebuilt by March 2029 at a cost of ¥8.6 billion. Why the left bank In September 2021, heavy rain upstream pushed the water at the Nishiki Bridge gauge to 4.9 metres, the highest since records began and well above the 4.6-metre danger level. The river overtopped the bank at Shimo-Kawabata and 1,140 homes were flooded, most of them in low-lying streets built on former rice paddies in the 1960s and 1970s. The first phase, between Asahi Bridge and Minato Bridge, rebuilt the stretch where the water came over. It was finished in March, on budget, at ¥2.9 billion. Phase 1 closed the gap where the river came through in 2021. But a bank is only as strong as its lowest point, and the lowest point is now downstream. — Satoshi Kudo, head of the Harvest Prefecture Mirror River Office Phase 2 costs ¥3.5 billion and will be carried out by Mirror Minato Construction JV, a joint venture of two local firms. The third and last phase, between Nishiki Bridge and Asahi Bridge, is the stretch of riverside used by the Lantern Festival. It is planned for April 2028 to March 2029, so that only one festival, in 2028, is affected. Path closed, lorries on Minato-dori From 1 October the path between Minato Bridge and the river mouth will be fenced off. Walkers and cyclists will be signed onto Minato-dori, which runs parallel to the river about 200 metres inland; the detour adds about 400 metres. Lorries carrying soil and steel will use Minato-dori on weekdays from 8:30 to 17:00, with up to 140 trips a day at the busiest stage next spring. There will be no night or weekend work, except in emergencies. The sheet piles will be pressed into the ground hydraulically rather than hammered, which the prefecture says will keep noise below 70 decibels at the nearest houses. At a briefing for residents at the Minatomachi community hall on 19 September, attended by about 120 people, several asked about safety on Minato-dori, which is also the route to Minatomachi Junior High School. The contractor said it would post guards at the two school crossings from 7:30 to 8:30 and from 15:00 to 17:00 on school days. I have walked my dog along the river every morning for 30 years. Eighteen months on Minato-dori with lorries is a long time. But I was here in 2021. I will take the lorries. — Toshio Yamane, 74, Minatomachi resident The closure also changes the course of the Springvale Castle Marathon in February, which will use Minato-dori between km 14 and km 18. A pump for the water that falls inside Raising the bank deals only with water coming from the river. In 2021 part of Shimo-Kawabata also flooded because rain falling behind the bank could not drain into a river that was already full. The city has proposed ¥1.1 billion in its September supplementary budget for a drainage pump station at Shimo-Kawabata that would lift 12 cubic metres of water a second over the bank. If the council approves the budget in its vote on 30 September, design work will start this autumn, with completion planned for fiscal 2028. Mirror River water levels at the Nishiki Bridge gauge Flood watch level: 3.2 m Evacuation decision level: 4.1 m Danger level: 4.6 m Record: 4.9 m (September 2021) Readings from the Nishiki Bridge gauge are published every ten minutes on the prefecture's river information website. The prefecture is asking residents near the river to check the city's flood hazard map, which was updated in April to reflect the Phase 1 works.

t: Comet to stop at Trailhead and run later at weekends from 14 November
s: Vale Rail's timetable revision adds a Comet stop at Trailhead, a later weekend last train from Moonview Spa, a later last train to Red Canyon on weeknights and a 15-minute midday service on the Bayside Line. The limited express will take two minutes longer.
x: Springvale Railway (Vale Rail) will revise the timetables of both its lines on Saturday 14 November, the company announced on Tuesday. Every Comet limited express will add a stop at Trailhead, the last train from Moonview Spa at weekends will leave 35 minutes later, and Bayside Line trains will run every 15 minutes instead of every 20 in the middle of weekdays. No services are being cut, and fares, Comet surcharges and pass prices stay the same. A new stop for the Comet At present the Comet stops only at Castle Town, Clayfield and Red Canyon between Springvale Central and Moonview Spa, and the journey takes 39 minutes. From 14 November all trains will also stop at Trailhead, 3.7 km short of the terminus, and the journey will take 41 minutes. About 420 passengers board at Trailhead on an average day, most of them on local trains that take about an hour to reach Springvale Central. Residents of the district around the station have asked for a limited express stop for years, and walkers heading for the trails on the eastern side of Mount Moonview often use the station. For us the Comet has always been a train that goes past the window. From November it is a train we can catch, and the city is a little over half an hour away. — Masako Hirata, who runs a guesthouse near Trailhead station The first weekday Comet, Comet 1, will leave Springvale Central at 7:25 instead of 7:30 and reach Moonview Spa at 8:06 instead of 8:09, so it still arrives before the start of the working day in the onsen town. Dinner before the last train At weekends and on holidays the last train from Moonview Spa now leaves at 21:05 and reaches Springvale Central at 22:08. From 14 November it will leave at 21:40 and arrive at 22:43, the same as on weekdays. The Moonview Spa Ryokan Association welcomed the later train. Day visitors who take a bath and stay for dinner often have to leave before dessert to catch the 21:05, it said, and some restaurants in the onsen town stop taking orders at 20:00 at weekends for that reason. Thirty-five minutes does not sound like much, but it is the difference between a rushed meal and a proper evening. — Shinji Oda, secretary of the Moonview Spa Ryokan Association Not everyone in the onsen town is pleased about the extra stop. Two of the association's members said the Comet's 39-minute run was its main selling point, and that a limited express which stops four times between the city and the terminus "is starting to look like a rapid". Later home for the upper valley On weekday nights the last northbound train from Springvale Central, at 23:20, now terminates at Clayfield. From 14 November it will run on to Red Canyon, arriving at 23:59. For passengers bound for Hilltop, Citrus Grove and Red Canyon, the last train will be 35 minutes later than the current 22:45. Rapid trains will also stop at Riverside, which they now pass. The stop adds one minute to the journey. About 4,120 passengers a day board at Riverside, and commuters there have until now had to take a local or change trains. We put trains where the passengers are. Trailhead, Riverside and the late train to Red Canyon are all places where people told us the timetable did not fit their lives. — Yoshiko Mae, managing director for operations, Vale Rail More trains to the port at midday On the Bayside Line, trains will run every 15 minutes instead of every 20 between 10:00 and 16:40 on weekdays. Ms Mae said midday trains between Springvale Central and Ferry Port had become noticeably fuller since the new blocks of flats near Ferry Port were finished. At weekends and on holidays the last eastbound train to Ferry Port now leaves Springvale Central at 23:00, and a later train at 23:35 runs only as far as Rose Garden. From 14 November the 23:35 will continue to Ferry Port, arriving at 0:03, so passengers for Tidewater, Lighthouse and Ferry Port will no longer need a taxi from Rose Garden. Vale Rail will publish the new station timetables on its website on 1 November. Comet seats for trains from 14 November can be reserved, as usual, from 10:00 one month before the day of travel, starting on 14 October; the company asks passengers to check the new times before booking. The timetable change at a glance Date: Saturday 14 November 2026 Comet: every train also stops at Trailhead; Springvale Central–Moonview Spa 41 min (now 39) Comet 1 (weekdays): 7:25 → 8:06 (now 7:30 → 8:09) Last train from Moonview Spa at weekends and on holidays: 21:40 (now 21:05) Last weekday train from Springvale Central, 23:20: runs to Red Canyon (now Clayfield) Rapid trains stop at Riverside Bayside Line, weekdays 10:00–16:40: every 15 min (now 20) Fares, surcharges and passes unchanged; new timetables online from 1 November

t: New Central Library to open on 7 November with 480,000 books and 640 seats
s: The ¥6.2 billion library next to Springvale Central Station will have more than three times as many seats as the 1974 building at Shiroyama, which closes on 18 October. There will be no lending from the central library for three weeks during the move.
x: Springvale's new Central Library will open on Saturday 7 November next to the South Exit of Springvale Central Station, the city Board of Education said on Friday, ending nearly a decade of planning and three years of construction. The five-storey building, with 9,800 square metres of floor space, replaces the Central Library at Shiroyama, which opened in 1974 and has long been too small for its collection: about a third of its books sit in closed stacks that readers must request at the counter. The new library can hold 620,000 volumes and will open with 480,000, about 410,000 moved from Shiroyama and 70,000 bought new. It has 640 seats, against 180 in the old building. Floor by floor Ground floor: café, new books and magazines, returns desk, and a 24-hour return box at the east entrance 2nd floor: children's library, with a story-time room and space for pushchairs 3rd floor: general collection and reading area 4th floor: local history collection and 12 study rooms that can be booked online 5th floor: rooftop terrace with views of Springvale Castle and Mount Moonview Self-service machines will let readers borrow books without queuing, and reserved books can be collected from lockers until 21:00. For fifty years people have told us the library is where they go when they have nowhere else to go. Now we can give them a seat. — Naoko Ishida, director of the Central Library Opening hours The library will stay open until 21:00 from Tuesday to Friday, two hours later than the Shiroyama building, and will close on Mondays. The move: three weeks without lending The Shiroyama library will close for good at the end of Sunday 18 October. From 19 October to 6 November there will be no lending from the central library while about 410,000 books are packed and moved. Books borrowed from 1 September onwards are all due back on 21 November, so nobody needs to return anything during the move. Books can still be returned to the six branch libraries, which stay open as usual, or to the return box at Shiroyama until 18 October. Library cards remain valid in the new building, and readers do not need to register again. Reservations made before 18 October will be kept. What it costs The building cost ¥6.2 billion: ¥5.4 billion for construction and ¥0.8 billion for fittings and furniture. This year's city budget puts ¥3.6 billion towards construction, the final payment, and ¥2.05 billion towards library services, up from ¥1.42 billion last year. The city has also proposed ¥0.6 billion in its September supplementary budget, which the council votes on on 30 September, for new books, computer systems and the move. Running the new library will cost about ¥1.31 billion a year, against ¥820 million for the old one, mainly because of the longer opening hours and 28 additional staff. Some councillors have questioned the running costs at a time when the city plans to raise water charges; the Board of Education expects visits to double to about 900,000 a year. What happens to Shiroyama? The future of the 1974 building, designed by a local architect and admired by some for its concrete reading hall, has not been decided. The city will decide by March 2027 whether to demolish it, sell it or find it a new use. A group of residents has asked for it to be kept as a community space. The new library has 40 parking spaces, most of them reserved for disabled visitors, and the city is asking readers to come by train, bus or bicycle. There is a bicycle park for 300 bikes under the building. Key dates 18 October (Sun): last day at the Shiroyama library 19 October – 6 November: no lending from the central library; branches open as usual 7 November (Sat): new Central Library opens 21 November: due date for all books borrowed from 1 September

t: Council passes ¥3.4 billion extra budget for flood pumps, school shelters and the new library
s: Springvale's general account for fiscal 2026 rises to ¥199.6 billion after the city council approved a September supplementary budget by 32 votes to 8. Here is where the money goes, where it comes from, and how spending on libraries has changed.
x: Springvale City Council on Wednesday approved a ¥3.4 billion supplementary budget, raising the city's general account for fiscal 2026, which runs from April 2026 to March 2027, to ¥199.6 billion. The vote, at the final plenary session before the mayoral election on 8 November, was 32 to 8 in the 40-seat council. The initial budget for the year, passed in March, was ¥196.2 billion, 3.1% more than the ¥190.3 billion of fiscal 2025 and the largest in the city's history. The September revision adds money for flood defences, school gymnasiums used as shelters, the opening of the new Central Library, help for small businesses facing higher energy bills, and safety at next week's Lantern Festival. What the extra ¥3.4 billion pays for The largest item, ¥1.1 billion, starts work on a drainage pump station at Shimo-Kawabata, the district where the Mirror River overtopped its banks in September 2021 and flooded 1,140 homes. The station's pumps will move 12 cubic metres of water a second into the river during heavy rain and are due to be finished in fiscal 2028. The pump station is the city's share of flood works; the embankment itself is a ¥8.6 billion Harvest Prefecture project. A further ¥0.9 billion will put air conditioning into the gymnasiums of 21 elementary and junior high schools that serve as evacuation shelters, by July 2027. Shelters in school gyms reached 35 °C during the evacuations of August last year, the city said. Every item in this budget answers a question residents asked us after 2021: will the water stay out, and where do we go if it doesn't? — Mayor Takuya Hirose The eight votes against came from the Mirror Citizens' Network group and two independents. Councillor Emi Tsuchiya said her group supported the pump station but not the timing. The pump station is necessary. But this budget was written for the election. There is nothing for older residents who can no longer drive, and nothing to soften the water rate rise we voted through the same afternoon. — Emi Tsuchiya, Mirror Citizens' Network Where the money goes Welfare and health remains by far the largest area of spending at ¥82.1 billion, 42% of the initial budget and ¥2.7 billion more than last year, mainly because of rising costs of care for older residents and the city's free childcare for children under three. Civil engineering, which covers roads, rivers and parks, rose by ¥1.1 billion to ¥22.9 billion. The biggest proportional rise is in culture, sport and libraries, up a third from ¥6.3 billion to ¥8.4 billion. Debt repayment fell from ¥19.7 billion to ¥19.2 billion, and commerce, tourism and labour from ¥7.2 billion to ¥6.9 billion after the end of a pandemic-era tourism voucher scheme. Libraries: up 44% Almost all of the increase for culture is the new Central Library, which opens on 7 November next to Springvale Central Station. Spending on library services, which covers staff, books and the running of the Central Library and six branches, rises from ¥1.42 billion in fiscal 2025 to ¥2.05 billion this year, an increase of 44%. Construction payments for the building rise from ¥1.9 billion to ¥3.6 billion, the last instalment of its ¥6.2 billion cost. The supplementary budget adds another ¥0.6 billion for opening the library: new books, the IT system and moving 480,000 volumes from the old library in Shiroyama. In all, the city will spend ¥6.25 billion on libraries this fiscal year. The new library's running costs are forecast at ¥1.31 billion a year, against ¥820 million for the old building. Where the money comes from City taxes, mainly residents' and property taxes, bring in ¥68.4 billion, or 34.9% of the initial budget. The rest depends heavily on Tokyo and the prefecture: ¥40.1 billion in national subsidies, ¥31.2 billion in local allocation tax and ¥14.6 billion in prefectural subsidies. New borrowing through municipal bonds is ¥17.3 billion. The city's outstanding debt stood at ¥214.5 billion at the end of fiscal 2025, or ¥519,600 for each of its 412,800 residents. "Other" revenue of ¥24.6 billion includes fees, the city's reserve fund and ¥3.8 billion of furusato nozei hometown tax donations received in fiscal 2025, most of them for gifts of yuzu and Springvale ware. Water rates passed the same day In a separate vote on Wednesday afternoon, the council approved the Waterworks Bureau's tariff revision by 29 votes to 11. Water and sewerage charges will rise by an average of 8.5% from 1 April 2027; a two-person household using 20 cubic metres every two months will pay ¥6,325 instead of ¥5,830. Both votes are likely to feature in the election campaign. Mayor Hirose is seeking a third term; his main challenger, former prefectural assembly member Michiko Sawada, has promised to review the water rise and to halve RideCard fares for residents aged 70 and over, paid for by the city. The budget in numbers Fiscal 2026 initial general account: ¥196.2 billion (+3.1%) September supplementary budget: ¥3.4 billion, passed 32–8 General account after revision: ¥199.6 billion Library services: ¥2.05 billion (fiscal 2025: ¥1.42 billion) City debt at end of fiscal 2025: ¥214.5 billion (¥519,600 per resident)

t: Herald poll: Hirose leads Sawada by five points, but one voter in five is undecided
s: Mayor Takuya Hirose is ahead in his bid for a third term, according to a Herald poll of 1,012 voters, but challenger Michiko Sawada leads among voters under 40, and flood control is the issue that matters most with five weeks to go.
x: Mayor Takuya Hirose holds a five-point lead over former prefectural assembly member Michiko Sawada in the race for Springvale City Hall, according to a poll conducted for The Springvale Herald on 26 and 27 September. Asked whom they would vote for if the election were held today, 36% of respondents chose Mr Hirose, 63, who is seeking a third four-year term. Ms Sawada, 55, was backed by 31%, and Ryo Onodera, 42, a former software company manager standing for the first time, by 12%. A further 21% said they had not decided. The lead is larger than the poll's margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, but with one voter in five undecided and the official campaign not starting until 1 November, the race remains open. A different race among younger voters The picture changes sharply among respondents aged 18 to 39. In that group Ms Sawada leads with 30%, followed by Mr Onodera on 27%, with Mr Hirose third on 22%. The share of undecided voters, 21%, is the same as in the poll as a whole. Hirose's lead rests on older voters, who turn out. Onodera is the wild card: if he holds a quarter of the under-40s, he takes votes Sawada needs. — Mai Kuroki, associate professor of political science, Springvale University Mr Onodera, who has no party or council group behind him, has campaigned mostly online, promising to put every city procedure online by 2028 and to cut the mayor's pay by 30%. Floods first, then the cost of living Asked which issue mattered most for their vote, 34% chose disaster prevention and flood control, ahead of the cost of living (27%), public transport (15%), childcare and education (11%) and the library and culture (4%). Nine per cent named another issue. The September 2021 flood, when the Mirror River overtopped at Shimo-Kawabata and flooded 1,140 homes, still shapes local politics. Among respondents who put flood control first, Mr Hirose led with 44%, ahead of Ms Sawada on 29%. Among those who named public transport, Ms Sawada led with 47%. Ms Sawada has made the cost of getting around part of her campaign: she has promised half-price RideCard fares for residents aged 70 and over, paid by the city. Mr Hirose's campaign says the pledge has not been costed. The candidates All three have announced their candidacy as independents. Mr Hirose is backed by the two largest council groups, the Civic Club and Mirai Springvale; Ms Sawada by the Mirror Citizens' Network. Five weeks is a long time. I will take the result as a reminder that nothing is won yet, and keep explaining what we have done on the river. — Takuya Hirose A five-point gap with a fifth of voters undecided is a race we can win. People are tired of being told fares and water bills are someone else's problem. — Michiko Sawada Mr Onodera said the poll showed that "a quarter of young people want something different from the two familiar names". Turnout and the campaign In 2022 Mr Hirose won re-election with 81,430 votes on a turnout of 41.8%. About 345,000 residents are eligible to vote this year. The official campaign runs from 1 to 7 November, and early voting is open from 2 to 7 November at City Hall and five branch offices. The Herald will host a debate between the three candidates on Thursday 22 October at 19:00 at Springvale Civic Hall. Tickets are free and the debate will be streamed on our website. Today the city council votes on the September supplementary budget and on the water rate rise, both of which Ms Sawada has criticised. How the poll was done Dates: 26–27 September 2026 Method: telephone, landline and mobile numbers chosen by random digit dialling Respondents: 1,012 eligible voters in Springvale Margin of error: ±3.1 points (larger for subgroups such as voters aged 18–39) Conducted by the Herald research desk

t: Water bills set to rise 8.5% from April, the first increase since 2009
s: A council committee has backed the Waterworks Bureau's plan to raise water and sewerage charges to pay for replacing ageing pipes. A typical two-person household would pay ¥495 more every two months. The full council votes on 30 September.
x: Springvale households will pay an average of 8.5% more for water and sewerage from 1 April 2027 if the city council approves a tariff revision at its plenary session on 30 September, after the council's construction and waterworks committee backed the plan on 18 September by seven votes to three. It would be the first rise since 2009. For a two-person household using 20 cubic metres every two months, the bill would go up from ¥5,830 to ¥6,325, an increase of ¥495. A single person using 10 cubic metres would pay ¥220 more, and a family of four using 40 cubic metres ¥930 more. Because the new tariff raises the charge per cubic metre more steeply for heavier use, a small shop using 100 cubic metres would face a 9.8% rise, or ¥2,750 every two months. Pipes older than the people using them The Waterworks Bureau says the rise is needed to replace pipes laid during the city's rapid growth in the 1970s and early 1980s. Of the 1,620 km of water mains under Springvale's streets, 31%, or about 500 km, are more than 40 years old, the legal service life for cast-iron and steel mains. The bureau plans to spend ¥64 billion over the next 20 years on replacement and earthquake-proofing, doubling the pace of work from about 13 km of mains a year to 25 km. At the current pace, it would take almost 40 years just to replace the pipes that are already past their service life. Pipe bursts are rising. The bureau recorded 46 bursts in fiscal 2025, up from 29 five years earlier. In February, a burst main under Otemachi-dori cut water to 2,100 households for 14 hours. We are not raising prices to balance the books this year. We are raising them so that in 2040 the water still comes out of the tap. — Hiroshi Nagai, director of the Springvale City Waterworks Bureau Fewer people, less water At the same time, revenue is falling. Water use in the city has dropped by 9% since 2015 as the population shrinks and households install water-saving appliances, and the bureau's income from charges fell to ¥11.8 billion in fiscal 2025. Without a rise, the bureau says its reserve fund would be used up by fiscal 2028. The bureau considered a two-stage rise of 5% in 2027 and 5% in 2029, but rejected it because it would cost more in total. A rise of 8.5% is expected to keep charges unchanged until at least 2031. What stays the same Households receiving public assistance will remain exempt from the basic charge, and the reduced rate for households with a family member who needs home dialysis will continue. The bureau will send every customer a leaflet with the new rates in January, and a bill calculator will be added to its website. What happens next 18 September: construction and waterworks committee approves the plan, 7–3 30 September: vote at the city council plenary session January 2027: leaflets with the new rates sent to all customers 1 April 2027: new charges take effect (first bill under the new tariff in June 2027) Opposition says timing is wrong The three committee members who voted against belong to the Mirror Citizens' Network. Councillor Emi Tsuchiya said the bureau should first spend part of its reserve and seek more national funding for pipe replacement. Prices of food, electricity and petrol are going up. Asking households for 8.5% more on top of that, with no plan to protect pensioners above the welfare line, is the wrong decision at the wrong time. — Emi Tsuchiya, Mirror Citizens' Network Michiko Sawada, the former prefectural assembly member who has announced she will run for mayor in November, said she would "review" the rise if elected. Mayor Takuya Hirose, who is seeking a third term, defended the plan at a press conference on Friday, saying that "putting off the bill only makes it larger for our children". Springvale's charges are in the middle of the range for cities of its size in western Japan. After the rise, a two-person household would still pay about ¥300 less every two months than in the prefectural capital, the bureau says.

t: Kumo Mobile to raise Unlimited plan by ¥220 from December
s: Kumo Unlimited will cost ¥7,458 a month from 1 December, and the Asia day pass for travellers abroad rises to ¥1,080. The other three plans and all discounts stay the same, and consumer advisers say users of less than about 25 GB a month may save by switching.
x: Kumo Mobile, the national carrier with its largest Harvest Prefecture shop in the Springvale Central Station building, said on Friday that it would raise the price of its Kumo Unlimited plan by ¥220 a month from 1 December. The company said it needed the extra revenue to keep investing in its 5G network as costs rise. Kumo Unlimited will go from ¥7,238 to ¥7,458 a month, tax included, a rise of 3.0%. The change applies to every Kumo Unlimited customer, including existing contracts, from December usage, which is the bill paid in January 2027. In a month when a customer uses 3 GB or less, the plan's low-use discount of ¥1,650 still applies, so the price for such a month rises from ¥5,588 to ¥5,808. The Kumo World day pass for Asia, which gives 24 hours of data abroad, rises from ¥980 to ¥1,080. Asia passes bought at the old price by 30 November can still be used until 31 January 2027. What stays the same Nothing else changes. Kumo Mini (3 GB, ¥2,178 a month), Kumo Basic (20 GB, ¥4,378) and Kumo 65+ (5 GB, ¥2,728) keep their prices, as do day passes for other parts of the world, call options and Device Care. All discounts stay as they are. That includes the family discount, which is worth more the more lines a family has. On Kumo Basic and Kumo Unlimited, each line gets ¥550 off a month in a group of two lines, ¥1,100 off with three lines and ¥1,210 off with four to ten. Kumo 65+ lines get ¥550 off however large the group, and Kumo Mini lines get no family discount. What it means for households For a single customer on Kumo Unlimited, the rise comes to ¥2,640 a year. A couple with two Unlimited lines will pay ¥13,816 a month after the family discount, up from ¥13,376. A family of three on Unlimited, each line with ¥1,100 off, will pay (¥7,458 − ¥1,100) × 3 = ¥19,074 a month, ¥660 more than now. We have kept every other price and every discount as it is. The change is limited to the plan that uses the most of the network. — Asami Fujita, Kumo Mobile spokesperson Kumo Mobile said it would tell affected customers by SMS and email during October. Check before you pay more Consumer advisers say the rise is a good moment for Unlimited users to look at how much data they really use. Kumo Basic includes 20 GB for ¥4,378, and extra data costs ¥550 per GB. A customer who uses 25 GB a month would pay ¥7,128 on Basic with five extra gigabytes, still less than the new Unlimited price; above about 25 GB, Unlimited is cheaper. The difference can be large. A customer who uses 18 GB a month and stays on Unlimited will pay ¥7,458 from December; on Kumo Basic the same customer would pay ¥4,378, or ¥3,080 less every month. Many people chose unlimited data years ago and never looked again. Your usage for the last three months is in the My Kumo app. If it is well under 25 GB, ask about Basic before December. — Yoko Ishikawa, counsellor at the Harvest Prefecture Consumer Centre Ms Ishikawa also warned that scam text messages pretending to come from mobile carriers tend to increase when prices change; Kumo Mobile itself warned customers about fake Kumo text messages last month. She advised customers not to follow links in messages about the price change and to check in the official app instead. Plan changes are free and there is no cancellation fee. A change made by 30 November takes effect on 1 December, so customers who switch in time will never pay the new Unlimited price. Kumo Mobile price change at a glance Kumo Unlimited: ¥7,238 → ¥7,458 a month from December usage (bill paid in January 2027) Unlimited in a month of 3 GB or less: ¥5,588 → ¥5,808 (low-use discount unchanged at ¥1,650) Kumo World Asia day pass: ¥980 → ¥1,080; passes bought by 30 November valid until 31 January 2027 No change: Kumo Mini, Kumo Basic, Kumo 65+, other day passes, call options, Device Care, all discounts Plan changes free; changes made by 30 November apply from 1 December At the Springvale Central shop Kumo Shop Springvale Central, on the second floor of the station building, is open every day from 10:00 to 20:00, with the last reception for new contracts and switching at 18:30. During the Lantern Festival on 10 and 11 October it stays open until 21:00. The shop recommends booking an appointment, as afternoon waits are long; plan changes can also be made in the My Kumo app. The rise follows the higher water charges approved by the city council on Wednesday, part of a run of price increases that has made the cost of living an issue in next month's mayoral election.

t: Springvale ware exports hit a record ¥2.84 billion as overseas buyers seek out small kilns
s: Exports of the city's pottery rose 22% last year and have more than tripled since 2016, led by the United States and France. But potters warn that the boom is stretching workshops with too few hands.
x: Exports of Springvale ware reached a record ¥2.84 billion in 2025, up 22% from ¥2.33 billion the year before, according to figures released by the Springvale Ware Cooperative. It was the fifth consecutive year of growth and more than three times the ¥0.92 billion exported in 2016. The cooperative's 63 member kilns, which employ 410 people, produced pottery worth ¥7.9 billion last year, meaning that more than a third of everything made in Springvale's kilns now leaves the country. The United States was the largest market, taking 31% of exports by value, followed by France with 18%, Taiwan with 14% and Australia with 9%. Other countries accounted for the remaining 28%. Exports fell to ¥0.97 billion in 2020, when restaurants and shops abroad closed during the pandemic, but have grown every year since. From tea bowls to dinner tables The growth has come less from the expensive tea bowls for which Springvale is known than from everyday tableware: rice bowls, small plates and cups in the blue-grey and amber ash glazes that buyers abroad now associate with the city. Restaurants in New York, Paris and Taipei that serve Japanese food have become regular customers, and several kilns sell directly to overseas shoppers through their own websites. Ten years ago a buyer from Paris would come once and order a few pieces for a gallery. Now they order two thousand rice bowls for a restaurant group and ask when the next batch is ready. — Hideo Maruyama, chair of the Springvale Ware Cooperative A weak yen has made Springvale pottery cheaper abroad, and the exhibition of four centuries of Springvale ware at the city's museum of art has drawn foreign visitors and buyers this autumn. Too few hands The success has exposed a problem the industry has talked about for years. Of the cooperative's 410 workers, almost half are over 60, and many kilns are run by a single family. Some have stopped taking new orders until next spring.

t: Ferry Port container traffic rebounds 6% as new Busan route and third crane take effect
s: The port handled 131,900 containers in the first eight months of 2026, recovering from a fall last fiscal year. Growth has picked up since a weekly service to Busan and Kaohsiung began in June.
x: Container traffic at Ferry Port rose 6.1% in the first eight months of 2026, recovering from a decline last year, according to figures published on Thursday by the Harvest Prefecture Port Authority. The port handled 131,900 TEU (twenty-foot equivalent units, the standard measure of container traffic) from January to August, up from 124,300 in the same period of 2025. In fiscal 2025, which ended in March, traffic fell 4.2% to 186,400 TEU from 194,600, after a shipping line ended its weekly service to Shanghai in May last year. Every month this year has been busier than the same month of 2025, but the gap widened after June, when a new weekly service linking Ferry Port with Busan in South Korea and Kaohsiung in Taiwan began. From January to May traffic was up 5.0%; from June to August it was up 7.8%. July, at 17,900 TEU, was the busiest month in the port's history. Busan gives our shippers a connection to the whole world in one stop. Before June, most of them sent containers by truck to Kobe or Hakata. — Kazuya Ota, director of the Harvest Prefecture Port Authority A third crane The port's third gantry crane went into service in September, after two years of construction work on the quay. The port authority says it will allow a container ship to be unloaded and loaded in about 14 hours instead of 20, and that it has already persuaded one more shipping line to consider calling at Springvale from next spring. Exports through the port include auto parts from factories in the Mirror valley, frozen fish and processed yuzu products, and a growing share of Springvale ware tableware, which reached a record ¥2.84 billion in exports last year. Imports are dominated by animal feed, building materials and furniture. Trucks and neighbours The growth has a cost for residents of Wangancho and Tidewater, the districts closest to the terminal. Truck traffic on the port access road rose by about 12% in the first half of the year, and residents' associations have asked the prefecture for a second access route.

t: Harvest Bay's eelgrass meadows grow back by 38% in ten years, university study finds
s: Springvale University researchers mapped 569 hectares of eelgrass in the bay in 2025, up from 412 hectares in 2015 and the largest area in more than 30 years. Cleaner water and 1.9 million shoots planted by fishers made the difference, they say, but hot summers could undo the gains.
x: The underwater meadows of Harvest Bay, which shrank to less than a third of their size in the second half of the 20th century, are recovering faster than expected, according to a study by Springvale University published this month in a peer-reviewed international journal of coastal ecology. A team led by Professor Emi Kanazawa of the university's Graduate School of Environmental Science found that eelgrass, known locally as amamo, covered 569 hectares of the bay in 2025. That is 38% more than the 412 hectares recorded in 2015 and the largest area since the early 1990s, although it is still less than half of the 1,240 hectares surveyed in 1978. From 1,240 hectares to 380 Eelgrass is a flowering plant that grows on sandy and muddy floors in shallow, clear water, usually less than five metres deep. Its meadows shelter young fish, squid and shellfish, trap sediment and store carbon in the sea floor. Older fishers in Springvale still call the shallows off Tidewater "the amamo field". The meadows declined steadily from the late 1970s as land was reclaimed for Ferry Port and industrial sites, and as nutrients from household waste water fed algae that clouded the water. By 2005 only 380 hectares were left. At the time, water transparency, measured by lowering a white disc into the sea until it can no longer be seen, averaged 3.1 metres at the bay's monitoring stations. When I started diving here as a student, you could swim for ten minutes over bare mud. Now, in places, you have to push your way through the leaves. — Professor Emi Kanazawa, Springvale University Cleaner water and 1.9 million shoots The study attributes the recovery to two changes. In 2012 the Harvest Bay treatment plant, which handles waste water for most of Springvale, introduced advanced treatment that removes much of the nitrogen and phosphorus. Transparency has since improved to an average of 4.6 metres in 2025, letting enough light reach beds that had been too dark for eelgrass to grow. The second change came from the water itself. Since 2011, members of the Harvest Bay Fishers' Cooperative have planted 1.9 million eelgrass shoots, raised from seed in tanks at the cooperative's hall and set by hand from small boats each spring and autumn. The researchers compared planted sites with bare sites of the same depth and sediment nearby, and found that planted sites were far more likely to grow into continuous meadows. We did it for the fish, not for a research paper. But it is good to see in numbers what we have been seeing from the boats for years. — Isamu Takeda, head of the Harvest Bay Fishers' Cooperative To map the meadows, the team combined drone and satellite images with dives at 120 survey points around the bay, where divers counted shoots and checked what the images showed. Figures for earlier years came from aerial photographs and prefectural surveys, which the team re-analysed with the same method so that the decades could be compared. The study in numbers Eelgrass area: 1,240 ha (1978), 380 ha (2005), 412 ha (2015), 569 ha (2025) Change since 2015: +157 ha, or +38% Water transparency: 3.1 m (2005), 4.6 m (2025) Shoots planted by the fishers' cooperative since 2011: 1.9 million Survey: 120 dive points, plus drone and satellite images Carbon dioxide absorbed: about 1,700 tonnes a year A carbon store that could earn money Eelgrass meadows lock carbon into the sediment beneath them, so-called blue carbon. The researchers estimate that Harvest Bay's meadows now absorb about 1,700 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. Springvale City's environment division said it is studying whether the meadows could earn blue carbon credits, which companies buy to offset their own emissions, and that any income would go back into the replanting programme. The fishers' cooperative currently spends about ¥4 million a year on seed, tanks and fuel, half of it covered by a prefectural grant. The returning meadows are already showing up in catches, Mr Takeda said. The cooperative's landings of young sea bream and of the small squid sold in Springvale's markets each spring have risen over the past five years, although the study did not measure fish numbers and Professor Kanazawa cautioned against drawing a direct line. Hot summers are the next threat The gains are fragile. In the summer of 2024, the temperature of the water in the shallows reached 30.8 °C, and the survey found that eelgrass had died back across parts of the bay shallower than two metres. Most of those beds recovered in 2025, but the team warns that repeated hot summers, and storms that tear plants from the sea floor, could reverse the trend. Eelgrass does not tolerate water above 28 degrees for long. If summers like 2024 become normal, the shallowest meadows will either move deeper or disappear. — Professor Kanazawa The team plans to repeat the full survey every five years and to place temperature loggers at 20 of the 120 points to monitor them each summer. The cooperative intends to shift its planting towards slightly deeper water, between two and four metres, from next spring. Professor Kanazawa will present the findings in a free public lecture at Springvale University's Kita Campus on Saturday 24 October at 14:00. No booking is required.

t: Flu season arrives six weeks early; city doubles vaccine subsidy for children
s: Harvest Prefecture declared the start of the influenza season on Thursday, about six weeks earlier than last year. Subsidised flu jabs begin at 212 clinics in Springvale on 1 October, with residents aged 65 and over paying ¥1,500 and the subsidy for children raised to ¥2,000 a dose.
x: Harvest Prefecture declared the start of this winter's influenza season on Thursday 24 September, about six weeks earlier than last year, after the number of patients reported by its sentinel clinics passed the threshold of 1.0 per clinic. In week 38 (14 to 20 September), the prefecture's sentinel clinics reported an average of 1.2 flu patients each. A preliminary count for the current week, released by the Harvest Prefecture Infectious Disease Surveillance Centre on Friday morning, put the figure at 1.8. At the same point last year it was 0.3, and the season was not declared until early November. Two classes at elementary schools in Springvale were closed this week after several pupils came down with flu, the city board of education said. Most cases so far have been type A. We usually see the first school closures in November. Seeing them in September tells us not to wait: if you are eligible, book your vaccination now. — Dr Akiko Noguchi, director of the Springvale City Public Health Centre Who pays what Springvale's subsidised vaccination programme runs from 1 October 2026 to 31 January 2027 at 212 clinics across the city. Residents aged 65 and over pay ¥1,500 for one dose. It is free for those in households receiving public assistance or exempt from resident tax, who must bring a certificate from the city. People aged 60 to 64 with a grade 1 heart, kidney, respiratory or immune disability are also eligible at ¥1,500 if they bring their disability certificate. For children, the city has doubled its subsidy. Children aged six months to 12 years need two doses, two to four weeks apart, and the city will now pay ¥2,000 towards each dose, up from ¥1,000 last season. Teenagers aged 13 to 18, who need only one dose, receive a ¥2,000 subsidy for the first time. Families pay the rest of the clinic's price, which in Springvale is usually between ¥3,500 and ¥4,500 a dose, so most will pay ¥1,500 to ¥2,500 after the subsidy. The same subsidy applies to the nasal spray vaccine for children aged 2 to 18, which is given as a single spray in each nostril instead of an injection. It is offered at 34 clinics only, and supplies are limited. The expanded children's subsidy will cost the city about ¥86 million this season, funded from the fiscal 2026 budget approved in March. Book early, bring your cards Most participating clinics take bookings by phone or online, and the public health centre expects the first two weeks of October to be busy. The list of clinics, with those offering the nasal spray marked, is on the city's website and available at the public health centre in Otemachi and at branch offices. What to bring Health insurance card or My Number card For children: the Maternal and Child Health Handbook, with the vaccination record For free vaccination: the public assistance or resident-tax exemption certificate For ages 60–64: the disability certificate The pre-vaccination questionnaire, filled in (available at clinics) Vaccine makers ship in batches through the autumn, and the city says it has been told supply will be about the same as last season. Dr Noguchi advised people not to wait for December: protection takes about two weeks to build up after the injection. Residents aged 65 and over can also receive this season's routine COVID-19 vaccination from 1 October, at a cost of ¥3,000. Most clinics can give both vaccines on the same day. If your child has flu Children diagnosed with flu must stay away from school until five days have passed since the symptoms began and two days have passed since the fever went down (three days for preschool children). The city reminds parents that its emergency clinic will stay open later for children from 1 October: see our report on the new night clinic hours. Hand-washing, fresh air and staying home with a fever still do a lot. The vaccine does not stop every infection, but it makes serious illness much less likely, especially for older people and small children. — Dr Noguchi

t: Children's emergency clinic to stay open until 23:00 from October
s: Springvale City Emergency Clinic will see children for an hour longer on weekdays and Saturdays, and drop its Sunday lunch break, from 1 October. Night visits by children reached a record 9,420 last year, and more than a thousand arrived after reception had closed.
x: Parents in Springvale will have an extra hour to take a sick child to a doctor in the evening from next month, when the city's emergency clinic extends its children's hours to 23:00 on every day of the week. From Thursday 1 October, the children's service at the Springvale City Emergency Clinic, on the ground floor of the Springvale Health Centre building in Otemachi, will open from 19:00 to 23:00 on weekdays, instead of closing at 22:00. On Saturdays it will open from 18:00 to 23:00. On Sundays and national holidays it will run continuously from 9:00 to 23:00, ending the lunch break between 12:00 and 13:00 that parents have long complained about. Reception will still close 30 minutes before the clinic does, at 22:30 on every day. A record year The clinic saw 9,420 children at night and at weekends in fiscal 2025, the year to March 2026, up 11% from 8,470 the year before and the highest number since it opened. The busiest hour on weekdays was between 21:00 and 22:00, which accounted for 28% of weekday visits. Last year 1,130 children arrived after reception had closed at 21:30 and were referred to Harvest Prefectural Central Hospital, whose children's emergency department is the only one in the city open overnight. The hospital says it treated 4,860 children at night in fiscal 2025, about 70% of whom had mild illnesses that a clinic could have handled. A child with a fever at 21:45 should not have to be driven to a hospital emergency department. Moving closing time to 23:00 covers most of the families who were being turned away. — Dr Makoto Ishii, head of the paediatric section of the Springvale Medical Association Doctors from local clinics take turns The clinic does not have its own paediatricians. It is staffed in rotation by 38 paediatricians from clinics around the city, who take evening and weekend shifts on top of their daytime work. The extra hour means about 360 more shifts a year, which the medical association agreed to cover after the city raised the hourly fee it pays doctors. The extension will cost about ¥42 million a year, including nurses, pharmacists and reception staff, and was included in the fiscal 2026 budget approved in March. The clinic's hours for adults are unchanged. Dr Ishii said the clinic expects a busy autumn. Cases of flu have been rising earlier than usual since late August, and the clinic usually sees its highest numbers from December to February. After 23:00, call #8000 first From 23:00 until the clinic opens again, parents who are unsure whether a child needs to see a doctor should call #8000, the children's medical helpline, which is answered by nurses and paediatricians from 18:00 to 8:00 every day. They can advise whether to wait until morning, go to hospital or call an ambulance. The duty hospital overnight remains Harvest Prefectural Central Hospital. In an emergency, such as a child who is struggling to breathe, having a seizure or cannot be woken, call 119 immediately. Before you go Hours from 1 October: weekdays 19:00–23:00, Saturdays 18:00–23:00, Sundays and holidays 9:00–23:00 Reception closes 30 minutes before closing time Bring the child's health insurance card, the city child medical subsidy card and the Maternal and Child Health Handbook Bring any medicine the child is taking, or its medicine notebook Treatment is free for children up to the end of junior high school who have the subsidy card After 23:00: call #8000; in an emergency, call 119 Parents welcome the change Parents' groups had asked the city to extend the hours for several years. A petition from a network of parents' associations at nursery schools collected 3,200 signatures in 2024. My son's fever went up after dinner and by the time we got there, reception had closed. We spent three hours at the hospital for something that needed ten minutes. An extra hour sounds small, but for us it would have changed everything. — Mother of two from Kitamachi The clinic does not take bookings. The city asks parents to phone ahead if possible, so that staff can tell them how long they are likely to wait.

t: Kuroda homer sends Seagulls into the final, first place two wins away
s: Daichi Kuroda's two-run home run in the first inning and two more runs in the seventh beat the Moonview Wild Boars 5–3 and clinched the Springvale Seagulls a place in the Shiokaze League final. Sunday's game has been postponed because of the typhoon.
x: Update, 11:20, Sunday 4 October: The Shiokaze League has postponed Sunday's 13:00 game between the Seagulls and the Wild Boars at Springvale Bayside Stadium because of Typhoon No. 21. It will now be played on Tuesday 6 October at 18:00. Tickets for Sunday's game are valid on Tuesday, or can be refunded at the stadium box office until 11 October. The Springvale Seagulls are in the Shiokaze League final. Daichi Kuroda hit a two-run home run in the first inning, Takumi Hoshino struck out seven in six innings, and the Seagulls beat the Moonview Wild Boars 5–3 at Springvale Bayside Stadium on Saturday night to make certain of a top-two finish with three games to play. The Aogiri Comets, who won 4–1 away at the Nishiura Tritons, have also clinched a place, so the final from 17 October will be the Seagulls against the Comets. What remains to be settled is who finishes first: the first-placed team hosts games one, two and, if needed, five of the best-of-five series. The Seagulls lead the Comets by two games, and their magic number for first place is two. Kuroda sets the tone The Seagulls wasted no time. Sota Imai singled to left with one out in the first, and Kuroda drove the next pitch he saw from Wild Boars starter Kosuke Ishiyama over the right-field fence. It was his 24th home run of the season, extending his lead at the top of the league, and his 81st run batted in. I was looking for a fastball after he missed with two sliders. With a crowd like this, on a night like this, you want to give them something to shout about early. — Daichi Kuroda The Wild Boars, who needed a win to keep alive their slim hopes of catching the Comets, cut the lead to 2–1 in the second on a sacrifice fly, and went ahead 3–2 in the fifth when their cleanup hitter Ryota Hayashi doubled into the left-centre gap with two men on. Hoshino, who had allowed only two runs in his previous 20 innings, settled down after that. He retired the last five batters he faced and left after six innings with six hits and three runs against him, seven strikeouts and two walks. Two in the seventh The Seagulls tied the game in the sixth. Yuto Sakai, who had two hits, doubled down the right-field line and scored on Shun Takagi's single up the middle. In the seventh, Kenji Arai drew a walk from Ishiyama and came home on Kaito Mori's single to centre to put the Seagulls back in front. After Ishiyama was replaced by Taro Nishi, Ren Matsuoka greeted the reliever with a single to right that brought Mori home for a 5–3 lead. Yamato Fujii pitched two scoreless innings, and closer Nao Kawabata gave up a two-out single in the ninth before ending the game on a fly ball to centre for his 19th save. Hoshino improved to 11–4. We said in spring that this team would play in October. Tonight is for the fans who have been coming here since we were last in the table. But we want first place, and we want to start the final at home. — Masaru Kitagawa, Seagulls manager Three games left The Seagulls' remaining games are Tuesday's rearranged home game against the Wild Boars at 18:00, a home game against the Shiomi Red Crabs on Saturday 10 October, which has been brought forward to 13:00 so that fans can get to the Lantern Festival in the evening, and the final regular-season game away at the Comets on Sunday 11 October. Two Seagulls wins, two Comets defeats, or one of each, will secure first place. If the Comets take all three of their games and the Seagulls win only one, the two teams would finish level, and first place would go to the Comets on their head-to-head record this season. The road to the final Tue 6 Oct, 18:00: Seagulls v Moonview Wild Boars, Springvale Bayside Stadium (postponed from 4 Oct) Sat 10 Oct, 13:00: Seagulls v Shiomi Red Crabs, Springvale Bayside Stadium (moved from 18:00) Sun 11 Oct: Aogiri Comets v Seagulls, away Final (best of five): from Sat 17 Oct; the first-placed team hosts games 1, 2 and 5 Saturday's crowd of 3,412 was the largest at Bayside Stadium this season. The Seagulls are averaging 2,870 spectators at home in 2026, up 9% on last year. The club said tickets for the first two games of the final will go on sale at the stadium and online on Monday 12 October at 10:00, priced from ¥1,500 for adults and ¥500 for children.

t: Castle Marathon entries open 1 October; course leaves the riverside for 4 km
s: The 11th Springvale Castle Marathon on 21 February 2027 has 7,000 full-marathon places, 2,000 of them reserved for residents, with a lottery if more apply. Embankment works on the Mirror River will move part of the course onto Minato-dori.
x: Entries for the 11th Springvale Castle Marathon open at 10:00 on Thursday 1 October, the organising committee announced on Tuesday. The race will be held on Sunday 21 February 2027, starting and finishing in Castle Park. There are 7,000 places in the full marathon, 3,000 in the 10 km race, 60 in the wheelchair 10 km and 500 pairs in the family 2 km. Entries close on 10 November or earlier if a category other than the full marathon fills up. If more than 7,000 people apply for the full marathon, places will be decided by lottery and runners told the result by 20 November. For the 2026 race, 11,800 people applied for the full marathon, and about three in five were successful. As in previous years, 2,000 full-marathon places are reserved for residents of Springvale, who are entered in a separate draw. The 2026 race, held in clear but cold weather, had 9,412 finishers across all four categories. The full-marathon course record of 2:13:48 was set in 2024. Riverside closed between km 14 and km 18 The course follows the same route as in recent years for most of its length: out of Castle Park, through the old town, along the Mirror River to Ferry Port and back. But between the 14 km and 18 km points, on the way out to the port, runners will leave the riverside path and run along Minato-dori instead. The change is needed because Harvest Prefecture plans to begin the second phase of its embankment works on the Mirror River on 1 October. The works, between Minato Bridge and the river mouth, will close the riverside walking and cycling path on that section until about March 2028. The organisers say the detour is almost exactly as long as the riverside section it replaces. To keep the course at 42.195 km, the turnaround point at Ferry Port will move about 150 metres, and the course will be re-measured in November for official certification. Runners loved the river stretch, and we will miss it for two years. But Minato-dori is wide and flat, and spectators can reach it more easily than the riverside path. — Yoko Shibata, secretary-general of the organising committee Minato-dori and the other roads on the course will be closed to traffic on race day from 8:00 to 15:10. Detailed closures and bus diversions will be announced in January. Fees, medals and charity places Entry fees are unchanged from last year: ¥13,000 for the full marathon, ¥6,500 for the 10 km, ¥3,000 for the wheelchair race and ¥3,000 per pair for the family run. Every finisher in the full marathon and 10 km receives a ceramic medal made by potters of the Springvale ware cooperative, each glazed by hand, so no two are the same. For the first time, 100 charity places in the full marathon will be offered outside the lottery for ¥50,000, of which ¥37,000 goes to a fund for cleaning up the banks of the Mirror River. Charity places are allocated in order of application. How to enter Entries: from 10:00 on Thursday 1 October to Tuesday 10 November 2026, on the official race website Full marathon: lottery if oversubscribed; results by 20 November; 2,000 places for city residents Residents must show proof of address when collecting their race number Number pick-up: 19 and 20 February 2027 at Springvale Civic Hall Race day: Sunday 21 February 2027; full marathon starts at 9:00 in Castle Park, time limit 6 hours Training season begins Local running clubs say they are already planning group runs for the winter. The Mirror Runners Club, which has 140 members, holds free practice runs from Castle Park at 7:00 every Sunday and welcomes beginners. February in Springvale can be very cold by the bay, but that is part of the charm. Start training in October and you will be ready. — Hiroki Sato, Mirror Runners Club Volunteers are also needed. The committee is looking for 2,200 people to help at water stations, the start and the finish, and along the course. Volunteer registration opens on 1 December.

t: "Fire and Earth" review: four centuries of Springvale ware, at its best and its most crowded
s: The City Museum of Art's 214-piece survey of the city's pottery is the most ambitious it has staged, with a superb Edo-period opening and a moving final room. Its middle sags under too many objects and too little explanation.
x: Rating: 4/5 It is hard to walk far in Springvale without meeting Springvale ware. It is on the counters of the noodle shops near the station, in the windows of Komachi-dori, in the gift catalogues that bring the city its furusato nozei donations. Familiarity can make a thing invisible. "Fire and Earth: Four Centuries of Springvale Ware", which opened at the Springvale City Museum of Art on 19 September and runs until 29 November, sets out to make us look again, and for the most part it succeeds. With 214 works borrowed from 31 lenders, including temples, private collectors, two national museums and the 63 kilns working in the city today, it is the largest exhibition the museum has mounted since it opened. It moves chronologically through six rooms, from the first kilns established under the castle lords in the early 17th century to work made this year. A jar worth the ticket The first two rooms are the strongest. The curators have resisted the urge to fill them, and the early pieces, mostly storage jars and plain bowls in the iron-rich local clay, have space to breathe. The thick, uneven ash glazes, running from grey-blue to amber where the flames hit them, look modern in a way that the later, more polished wares do not. At the centre of the second room, alone in a free-standing case, is the so-called Moonview jar, made in the 1680s and lent by a temple in the hills below Mount Moonview. It is about 50 centimetres tall, slightly lopsided, with a pale glaze that has gathered into a glassy green pool on one shoulder. Legend says the potter left it in the kiln a day too long. Whatever happened, the result is the finest single object I have seen in a Springvale museum, and it alone is worth the ¥1,200 ticket. The jar has not been shown in public for 26 years. The temple agreed to lend it on condition that it travels nowhere else. — Chief curator Shigeru Okabe The tea bowls of the third room are quieter but rewarding: look for the small group made for the castle lords' tea gatherings, with their thumb-shaped dents and a pale crackle glaze. Too much of the Meiji boom The exhibition stumbles in room four, devoted to the export wares made after Japan opened its ports. In the 1880s and 1890s, Springvale workshops produced huge vases, dinner services and decorative plates for buyers in Europe and America, painted with birds, flowers and the occasional startled tiger.
