The story is important: it was the first time Springvale's potters made their living from abroad, as they increasingly do again today. But the curators have crammed more than 60 pieces into a room smaller than the first, and the effect is of a very good antique shop. Labels are small, set low and in grey type that is hard to read in the dim light. English labels, generous in the first two rooms, become a single short panel here. Most of all, I missed the people: who painted these plates, how they were paid, and what happened to the workshops when demand collapsed after the First World War. A moving final room The last two rooms recover the momentum. Room five traces the 20th-century decline, when the number of kilns fell below 20, and the revival led by potters who returned to local clay and wood firing from the 1960s. Room six is given over to contemporary work, including pieces by potters still in their twenties who sell mainly to buyers abroad. A wall of 120 everyday cups, one from each of the city's working potters past and present, which visitors are told they may touch, is a simple idea that gets the whole exhibition right: Springvale ware was always meant to be used. We wanted people to leave holding a cup, not just looking at a jar behind glass. — Shigeru Okabe The catalogue (¥2,800) is excellent, with new photographs of every work and an essay on the clay pits of the Mirror valley. The audio guide (¥600) is narrated in Japanese and English and is worth it for the first three rooms. Practical information Where: Springvale City Museum of Art, Castle Park (12 minutes' walk from Springvale Central Station) When: until Sunday 29 November 2026 Hours: 9:30–17:00, Fridays until 20:00; last entry 30 minutes before closing Lantern Festival: open until 21:00 on Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October Closed: Mondays (open on Monday 12 October, a national holiday, and closed on Tuesday 13 October instead) Admission: adults ¥1,200; university students ¥800; high-school students and younger free Works on paper and kiln records in room 2 change on 27 October Verdict "Fire and Earth" is not perfect. The export room needs half its objects and twice its explanation, and visitors with less than perfect eyesight will struggle with the labels throughout. But at its best, in the Edo rooms and in that final wall of cups, it does what a local exhibition should: it sends you back into the city's shops and kitchens seeing the familiar as if for the first time. Go on a weekday morning, start slowly, and save some energy for the end.

t: Typhoon No. 21 set to pass close to Springvale early on Monday
s: The storm is forecast to bring gusts of up to 45 m/s, as much as 250 mm of rain in the mountains and a storm surge timed with Monday's high tide. Warnings are likely from Sunday afternoon, and Vale Rail will decide on Sunday afternoon whether to stop its trains.
x: Typhoon No. 21 is expected to pass close to Springvale in the early hours of Monday 5 October. It is likely to bring the strongest winds the city has seen in several years, heavy rain across Harvest Prefecture and a storm surge along Harvest Bay. At 15:00 on Saturday the typhoon was about 650 km south-south-west of Springvale, according to the Harvest Local Meteorological Observatory. Its central pressure was 960 hPa, with sustained winds of up to 35 m/s and gusts of up to 50 m/s. It was moving slowly north at about 10 km/h, but the observatory expects it to turn north-north-east on Sunday and speed up, keeping its strength as it crosses warm sea. Closest at about 04:00 on Monday In the observatory's central forecast the centre comes within about 30 km of Springvale at around 04:00 on Monday, passing to the west of the city before moving inland and weakening during the day. The forecast circle for Monday morning is still about 200 km across, so the track may yet shift. A track to the west matters. A typhoon's strongest winds are on its eastern side, where its own winds add to the speed at which it is moving. A track just to the west puts the whole city on the dangerous side of the storm. Prepare on Saturday and on Sunday morning, not on Sunday night. — Yumi Kaneko, forecaster, Harvest Local Meteorological Observatory Wind, rain and the tide Rain is expected from Sunday morning and should become heavy by Sunday evening. In the 24 hours to Monday evening the observatory expects 150–200 mm in the city and up to 250 mm in the mountains around Mount Moonview, with up to 40 mm in an hour at the peak. Mean winds could reach 25–30 m/s, with gusts of 40–45 m/s, strongest between midnight and 06:00 on Monday. Waves of up to 6 m are forecast in Harvest Bay. The timing is the main worry along the bay. High tide on Monday is at 05:12, about an hour after the typhoon's closest approach. The observatory says the sea could rise more than 2 m above its standard level along the coast at Minatomachi, Wangancho and Tidewater. Storm, heavy rain and high wave warnings are likely to be issued on Sunday afternoon, and a storm surge warning on Sunday evening. Check the latest on our weather page. The Mirror River Rain that falls in the mountains reaches the lower Mirror River six to nine hours later. The prefecture watches the gauge at Nishiki Bridge, where 3.2 m is the flood watch level, 4.1 m the level at which the city considers evacuation, and 4.6 m the danger level. In the September 2021 flood the gauge reached a record 4.9 m and the river overtopped its bank at Shimo-Kawabata, flooding 1,140 homes. Since then the left bank has been raised by 1.0 m along the 1.1 km between Asahi Bridge and Minato Bridge. Work on the second section, down to the river mouth, began only on Thursday, and the stretch through the city centre, between Nishiki Bridge and Asahi Bridge, is not due to be strengthened until 2028 (our report on the works). What the city and Vale Rail plan The city's Disaster Management Office said it was likely to issue a Level 3 alert on Sunday afternoon, asking older people and anyone who needs help to move to go to a shelter, and that shelters would open at the same time. If the river or the tide rises faster than forecast, a Level 4 evacuation instruction for low-lying districts could follow on Sunday evening. Sandbags are available free at City Hall and the five branch offices until 17:00 on Saturday and from 9:00 to 15:00 on Sunday. Springvale Railway (Vale Rail) said it was considering stopping trains on Sunday evening and would announce its decision at 15:00 on Sunday. Until then, trains run to the weekend timetable. Ferries from Ferry Port are likely to be cancelled from Sunday morning. Lantern Festival organisers will take down the 4,000 lanterns already hung along the river on Sunday morning. The festival itself, on 10 and 11 October, is not expected to be affected: the forecast for next Saturday is sunny, with a high of 23 °C. Before the storm Bring in or tie down anything on balconies and in gardens Keep three days of drinking water and food; charge phones and power banks Check the city hazard map for your address and the way to your nearest shelter Keep medicine, documents and a torch in one bag Do not go to look at the river or the sea during the storm We will follow the typhoon in our live coverage from Saturday evening.

t: Editorial: The river will not wait until 2029
s: The stretch of the Mirror River embankment that runs through the heart of Springvale is the last in line to be strengthened. The prefecture and the city should bring it forward, and every candidate for mayor should say how.
tags: Mirror River Disaster prevention Mayoral election 2026
x: Five years ago last month, the Mirror River rose to 4.9 m at the Nishiki Bridge gauge, the highest level ever recorded there. It overtopped its bank at Shimo-Kawabata and flooded 1,140 homes. Many families in that district spent the following winter in temporary housing; some never returned. Since then, Harvest Prefecture has done much of what it promised. The first phase of its ¥8.6 billion programme to strengthen 3.2 km of the left bank, the 1.1 km between Asahi Bridge and Minato Bridge, was completed in March, on time and within its ¥2.9 billion budget. The crest is now 1.0 m higher, at 7.4 m, backed by steel sheet piles and a 12 m berm. The second phase, from Minato Bridge to the river mouth, began on Thursday. It will cost ¥3.5 billion and close the riverside path there until about March 2028. Walkers, cyclists and the runners of next February's Castle Marathon will have to take Minato-dori instead. That is a price worth paying. The wrong way round The problem is the order. The third phase, the 0.9 km between Nishiki Bridge and Asahi Bridge, is not due to start until April 2028, and will not be finished until March 2029. This is the stretch that runs past the old town, Castle Park and the riverside where 300,000 people will gather for the Lantern Festival next weekend. City Hall is a few hundred metres away. It is, in short, the stretch where a breach would do the most harm. The prefecture's Mirror River Office gives three reasons for the timetable: the contractor can work on only one section at a time; the trucks for both sections would have to share narrow roads; and national subsidies are spread over several years. We do not dismiss these. But none of them prevents the prefecture from starting the survey and design work for Phase 3 now, so that construction can begin the moment Phase 2 allows. Nor do they rule out strengthening the most vulnerable few hundred metres of Phase 3 first, during the dry winter months of 2027. The city's part The city has its own work to do. This week the council approved ¥1.1 billion in the September supplementary budget for a drainage pump station at Shimo-Kawabata, able to pump 12 cubic metres a second out of the low-lying streets into the river. That is welcome. But the pumps will not be ready until fiscal 2028, and a pump station behind a weak embankment protects only half of what it should. Springvale is not a rich city. Its debt stands at ¥214.5 billion, or ¥519,600 for every resident, and the cost of the new library is still being paid off. We understand why the mayor and the council are cautious. But the city could offer the prefecture something concrete: a share of the design costs for Phase 3, or the use of city land for a second construction yard so that two sections can be worked at once. Money spent before a flood buys far more than money spent after one. Money spent before a flood buys far more than money spent after one. A question for the candidates The mayoral election on 8 November gives voters a chance to ask. In our poll last week, 34% of respondents named disaster prevention and flood control as the most important issue for their vote, ahead of the cost of living at 27% (poll report). All three candidates say they will keep the city safe. Only one, Mayor Takuya Hirose, makes the embankment and the pump station a headline pledge, and even he has not said whether he would press the prefecture to change its timetable. We ask each candidate to answer two questions before our debate at Springvale Civic Hall on 22 October. In what year will the embankment through the city centre be finished? And what will the city pay to make that happen? As this editorial goes to press, Typhoon No. 21 is moving north towards Harvest Prefecture, and the observatory expects it to pass close to the city early on Monday (forecast). We hope the river stays within its banks. But hope, and luck, are not a flood defence. The next flood will not check the prefecture's timetable first.

t: A timetable is a promise
s: Vale Rail's November timetable slows its flagship train by two minutes so that a small station can catch it. That is the right instinct. The question is who the next revision remembers.
x: My mother is 84 and lives in the upper Mirror valley. She does not own a timetable. She has never needed one: she knows the last train home, and she knows that if she misses it, she sleeps at my house. From 14 November, under the timetable revision Vale Rail announced on Tuesday, several of those small certainties shift. Every Comet limited express will stop at Trailhead, a station where about 420 people board a day, and the run from Springvale Central to Moonview Spa will take 41 minutes instead of 39. The weekday last train at 23:20 will go on past Clayfield to Red Canyon. Rapids will stop at Riverside. At weekends the last train down from Moonview Spa will leave at 21:40 instead of 21:05, and the Bayside Line will run every 15 minutes in the middle of weekdays. Two minutes is the price of the Trailhead stop, and some in the onsen town have already complained that their fast train is becoming slower. I think the two minutes are the best thing in the revision. A limited express exists to sell speed to visitors; when it stops for a village of a few thousand people, the railway is remembering that it also serves the people who live along its line. That is what a timetable really is. Not a schedule but a promise about how a place works: this is when you can leave, this is when you can come home, this is how late you can stay out and still sleep in your own bed. Every line of the November timetable is a promise to someone: to the innkeepers who want their guests to finish dinner, to the night-shift workers of Red Canyon, to the families in the new flats by the port. So it is worth asking who received no new promise.

t: What a library is for
s: The new Central Library will be a magnificent building. But for 52 years the old library at Shiroyama has offered something a building alone cannot: a public place you can walk to.
x: I first walked into the library at Shiroyama in the spring of 1974, a few weeks after it opened. I was eleven, and I remember the smell of new shelves and the librarian who let me take out four books when the limit was three. Thirty-four years as a school librarian in this city began, I think, at that counter. Next month the city opens its new Central Library beside Springvale Central Station, and the old building closes its doors for the last time on 18 October. I have been inside the new one on a tour for former staff, and I want to say plainly: it is wonderful. Five floors and 9,800 square metres. Room for 620,000 books. A whole floor for children, study rooms on the fourth floor, a café, and a rooftop terrace from which, on a clear day, you can see Mount Moonview. Most of all, 640 seats. Anyone who tried to find one of the old library's 180 seats in January, when every secondary school pupil in the city is revising, will know what that means. A fair price The building cost ¥6.2 billion, and it will cost about ¥1.31 billion a year to run, compared with ¥820 million for the old library. Some readers have written to this newspaper to say that is too much. I disagree. A library is the only indoor public place in this city where nobody asks you to buy anything, prove anything or leave by a certain time. It serves the child with nowhere quiet to do homework, the pensioner reading the newspapers, the job-seeker printing a CV, the visitor waiting for a train. Per resident, ¥1.31 billion is little more than ¥3,000 a year. I cannot think of a better bargain in the city budget. A library is the only indoor public place in this city where nobody asks you to buy anything, prove anything or leave by a certain time. What Shiroyama loses My worry is not the new library. It is the neighbourhood it leaves behind. Shiroyama is an old district on a hill. Many of the people who use its library are over seventy, and for them the station is not a short walk but a bus ride each way. The six branch libraries will stay open, but none of them is in Shiroyama. The city says it will decide what to do with the old building by March next year. I would ask the city to consider something modest. Keep one room of the old building open as a small reading room and lending point, with a few thousand books, the daily newspapers, and a librarian two or three days a week. Let readers order books from the Central Library and collect them there. It would cost a small fraction of the new building's running costs, and it would mean that the opening of one library does not mean the closing of another. Remember the schools One more request. The new library will have a children's floor, and that is good. But most children meet books first in school libraries, and in this city many of those are open only when a teacher can spare the time. Of the 59 elementary and junior high schools in Springvale, fewer than half have a school librarian for more than two days a week. If the city can find ¥6.2 billion for a building, it can find a little more for the people who teach children to use one. I will be at the opening in November, I expect with a great many others. I will also be at Shiroyama on 18 October, to say goodbye to the counter where I took out four books instead of three. Both buildings, in their way, are what a library is for.

t: Correction: the new Central Library opens on 7 November
s: An article published on 26 September gave the wrong opening date for the new library next to Springvale Central Station.
x: In our article on the new Springvale Central Library, published on 26 September, we said that the library next to the South Exit of Springvale Central Station would open on 3 November. That was wrong. The library opens on Saturday 7 November 2026. The other dates in the article were correct: the old library at Shiroyama closes on Sunday 18 October, there is no lending from the central library from 19 October to 6 November, and all books borrowed from 1 September onwards are due back on 21 November. The article has been corrected. We apologise for the error, and thank the readers who pointed it out. Our corrections policy and a list of recent corrections are on the corrections page.

t: Typhoon No. 21 live: evacuation instruction for four districts as the storm nears Springvale
s: The typhoon is expected to pass about 30 km west of the city around 04:00 on Monday. Storm and storm surge warnings are in force, trains stop this evening and 24 shelters are open. The latest updates are below, newest first.
tags: Typhoon No. 21 Disaster prevention Springvale Railway Transport
x: Bayside Line stops at 18:00; last Mirror Line train at 19:15. Vale Rail says the last Bayside Line trains have left: the 17:40 from Springvale Central (due at Ferry Port at 18:08) and the 17:50 from Ferry Port (due at Springvale Central at 18:18). No Bayside Line trains will start after 18:00. On the Mirror Line, the last train from Springvale Central to Moonview Spa leaves at 19:15 and arrives at 20:18; the last train from Moonview Spa leaves at 18:40. After about 20:20 no Mirror Line trains will run. Staff at Springvale Central said the platforms were busy but calm. The Comet limited express remains cancelled until at least noon on Monday. Vale Rail will decide at 10:00 on Monday, after inspecting the track, when services restart. 1,284 people in shelters. Pets are allowed, in cages, at the Civic Gymnasium, the Wangancho Community Centre, Springvale University Kita Campus Hall and three smaller shelters. Power restored in Minatomachi. Its repair crews will stop work once mean winds pass 20 m/s, so any further cuts tonight may not be fixed until Monday morning. Level 4: evacuation instruction for four districts. The city has issued an evacuation instruction (Level 4) for Shimo-Kawabata, Minatomachi, Wangancho and Tidewater, covering 12,480 households and 27,300 people, because of the risk of storm surge and of the Mirror River rising. Everyone in these districts should leave now for a shelter or a safe place outside the area. If going out is already dangerous, move to an upper floor on the side of the building away from the sea and the river. Do not wait for the wind. In two hours it may be too dangerous to walk to a shelter. — Kazuo Tamura, head of the City Disaster Management Office Storm surge warning issued. The observatory has issued a storm surge warning for the Harvest Bay coast. The tide could rise up to 2.4 m above its standard level between 04:00 and 06:00 on Monday, around the high tide at 05:12 and soon after the typhoon's closest approach. Low-lying parts of Minatomachi, Wangancho and Tidewater are most at risk. Mirror River at 2.6 m and rising. The Nishiki Bridge gauge read 2.6 m at 17:00, up from 1.9 m at 14:00 (about 1.2 m on a normal day). The prefecture forecasts a peak of about 4.3 m around 06:00 on Monday. That is above the 4.1 m level at which the city considers evacuation, but below the 4.6 m danger level. The record, set in September 2021, is 4.9 m. Power cut in Minatomachi. About 380 households in Minatomachi lost power at 16:50 after a tree fell on a line near Minatomachi Junior High School. The city says the shelter at the school has its own generator and is unaffected. Storm warning issued for Springvale. The observatory has issued a storm warning for Springvale. Mean winds could reach 30 m/s and gusts 45 m/s from late this evening until Monday morning, strongest around 04:00. Winds that strong can overturn lorries, break windows and bring down utility poles. Stay indoors from this evening and keep away from windows. Bay bridge closed; city buses stop at 19:00. Harvest Bay Bridge closed to all traffic at 16:00 because of strong crosswinds. The city transport bureau says all city buses will stop at 19:00; on most routes the last buses from Springvale Central leave between 18:20 and 18:40. Ferry Port ferries remain cancelled today and on Monday. Typhoon 420 km away and speeding up. At 15:00 the typhoon was about 420 km south-south-west of Springvale, with a central pressure of 955 hPa, maximum winds of 40 m/s and gusts of 60 m/s. It is moving north-north-east at 25 km/h and is expected to speed up overnight. Storm-force winds (25 m/s or more) extend 150 km from the centre on its eastern side, and gales 500 km. The observatory still expects the centre to pass about 30 km west of the city around 04:00 on Monday, which would put Springvale on the stronger, eastern side. See the track map on our weather page. Heavy rain warning. A heavy rain warning for landslides and inundation is now in force. Up to 40 mm of rain an hour is possible overnight, with 170 mm in the city and 250 mm in the mountains in the 24 hours to 18:00 on Monday. Slopes in the Moonview area and the hills behind Shiroyama are most at risk of landslides. Vale Rail announces evening suspensions. Springvale Railway says it will stop its trains this evening, ahead of the typhoon: Comet: the last trains today are the 15:30 from Springvale Central (Moonview Spa 16:09) and the 15:50 from Moonview Spa (Springvale Central 16:29). The 17:30 and 19:30 from Springvale Central and the 16:50, 17:50 and 19:50 from Moonview Spa are cancelled, and so are Monday's Comet until at least noon. Bayside Line: suspended from 18:00. Last eastbound train: 17:40 from Springvale Central (Ferry Port 18:08). Last westbound: 17:50 from Ferry Port (Springvale Central 18:18). Mirror Line: last train from Springvale Central to Moonview Spa at 19:15 (arrives 20:18); last from Moonview Spa at 18:40 (Springvale Central 19:43). No Mirror Line trains after about 20:20. Tickets for cancelled Comet trains will be refunded without a fee at any Vale Rail ticket office until 4 November. Vale Rail will decide at 10:00 on Monday, after inspecting the track, when services restart. Level 3: older people should move now; 24 shelters open. The city has issued a Level 3 alert (evacuation of older people and others who need time to move) for the whole city and opened 24 shelters. People who are older, disabled, pregnant or caring for small children should start moving now, to a shelter or to relatives in a safe area. Everyone else should get ready to leave. Bring medicine, water, food for one day, a phone charger and a blanket. Flood advisory for the Mirror River. A flood advisory is now in force for the Mirror River. The Nishiki Bridge gauge read 1.9 m at 14:00. Rain in the mountains reaches the city stretch of the river six to nine hours later, so the river is expected to keep rising until Monday morning. Mirror Line delays after a train hits a deer. At 13:52 a southbound Mirror Line train hit a deer between Mill Creek and Firefly Valley. Trains between Red Canyon and Moonview Spa are running up to 25 minutes late, and the Comet 18 (Moonview Spa 14:50 to Springvale Central) is about 20 minutes late. Vale Rail expects normal service from around 15:40. The Bayside Line is running normally. The company will announce at 15:00 whether it will stop trains this evening because of the typhoon. Rubbish, hospital and station shops. Monday's rubbish collection is cancelled in all districts. Please keep rubbish indoors. Harvest Prefectural Central Hospital will close its outpatient clinics on Monday morning. Emergency care continues as normal. Shops in the Springvale Central station building close at 17:00 today. Schools closed on Monday. All city elementary and junior high schools will be closed on Monday, the Board of Education says. Springvale University has cancelled all classes on Monday. Decisions about Tuesday will be made on Monday afternoon. City sets up disaster headquarters. The city has set up its disaster response headquarters at City Hall. Mayor Takuya Hirose told reporters that the city expected to issue a Level 3 alert at 15:00. If you live near the sea or the river, or you need help to move, do not wait for an instruction. Go while it is still light. — Mayor Takuya Hirose High wave warning; ferries cancelled. A high wave warning is now in force, with waves of 6 m in Harvest Bay and 8 m offshore. All Ferry Port ferry services are cancelled today and on Monday. All riverside lanterns taken down. Festival volunteers finished taking down the 4,000 lanterns along the Mirror River at 10:40. They are stored at the festival workshop in the former Riverside textile warehouse and will be put back between 6 and 9 October. The executive committee will say on Thursday 8 October at 15:00 whether the festival on 10 and 11 October goes ahead in full. Festival road closures and plans Embankment works site secured. The contractor for the second phase of the Mirror River embankment works, Mirror Minato Construction JV, has moved its excavators and materials from the riverbank to the top of the levee, the prefecture says. The work, which began on Thursday below Minato Bridge, is suspended until the river falls. Seagulls game postponed. Tickets for today are valid on Tuesday. The Seagulls clinched a playoff place last night (match report). Thunderstorm advisory. A thunderstorm advisory is in force for Springvale until Monday afternoon. Lightning and sudden gusts are possible as the first rain bands arrive. Trains running normally; Vale Rail to decide at 15:00. Springvale Railway says all its trains, including the Comet limited express, are running normally this morning on the weekend timetable. It will announce at 15:00 whether it will stop trains this evening, and expects any suspension to start around 18:00 at the earliest. If you plan to travel this afternoon, check before you set out. Volunteers start taking down the lanterns. About 200 volunteers and festival staff began removing the lanterns along Riverside Avenue at 7:00, in light rain. "We built them in 40 days. We can take them down in a morning," one volunteer said. Typhoon 520 km away. At 06:00 the typhoon was about 520 km south-south-west of Springvale, with a central pressure of 958 hPa, moving north-north-east at 15 km/h. Rain is expected to spread across the city from late morning and become heavy this evening. Lanterns to come down on Sunday morning. The Lantern Festival Executive Committee has confirmed that the 4,000 lanterns already hung along the Mirror River will be taken down from 7:00 on Sunday. Riverside Avenue stays open during the work; drivers should take care. Live coverage begins.
